title: AI Researching the Future of Education 2026
author: Rupert Wegerif
source: Expanding Dialogic Space with Rupert Wegerif (rupertwegerif.substack.com), August 17,
summary: Rupert Wegerif challenges the increasingly common claim that AI use straightforwardly damages student learning, arguing that the research producing this conclusion is methodologically narrow: it measures 'learning' only as performance on existing curricula and standard assessments completed without AI. Using the Bastani et al. randomized controlled trial as his central example, he shows that students who lost access to an unrestricted AI assistant scored worse on conventional tests, but argues this proves only that unrestricted AI didn't prepare them for an AI-free exam, not that AI damaged their underlying capacity to think. He proposes design-based research as an alternative to the medical-trial model borrowed from psychology, one that asks not just whether an intervention improves test scores but whether it should change what we consider learning to be in the first place. A Japanese university study on AI-assisted classroom design serves as his model: it revealed that AI is good at generating possibilities but that judgment, selection, and coherent synthesis remain distinctly human capacities worth deliberately teaching. Wegerif's larger argument is that educational research cannot settle questions of purpose the way natural science settles empirical questions, and that evidence must feed into ongoing dialogue about what education should aim for rather than replace that dialogue.
points: Reframes the Bastani et al. finding that AI hurt post-AI test performance as evidence about test design, not proof that AI erodes underlying mathematical capability, using an abacus/calculator analogy to expose the assumption embedded in the original study.

Argues that most educational-technology research quietly assumes the existing curriculum and its standard assessments define 'learning,' which forecloses investigation of new capacities AI interaction might require or produce.

Uses a Japanese design-based study of AI-assisted classroom design to show that widening the pool of ideas with AI does not automatically improve synthesis; the missing skill was judgment and selection, not idea generation.

Proposes design-based research (testing whether an intervention produces the anticipated process, and whether that process should even count as the goal) as a rigorous alternative to import from the medical RCT model.

Insists education's core questions ('what should we teach and how') are not answerable by empirical research alone, positioning research as a contributor to dialogue about educational purpose rather than a final arbiter.
quotes: Students given access to an unrestricted GPT-4-based assistant performed substantially better while using it. But when the AI was removed, they scored 17 per cent lower than students who had studied using conventional resources. The influential conclusion: generative AI can improve performance while undermining learning.

Imagine a mathematics class where students learn to calculate using an abacus and use it in exams. An experimental group gets calculators during lessons, but must use an abacus in the final exam. If they perform worse, we might conclude that calculator use didn't prepare them to operate an abacus.
Instead of asking whether a tool improves existing test scores, it asks: Does design X generate the anticipated process M? Did that process contribute to the intended outcome Y?

The intervention did produce 'idea expansion': students generated possibilities that went beyond the original materials. Yet relatively few groups turned this expanded range into coherent, genuinely innovative proposals.

The fundamental questions of education differ from those of natural science. They are not 'does this work?' but 'what should we teach and how should we teach it?' Empirical research cannot answer that alone.
